title: Differentiarum Sive De Proprietate Sermonum Libri Duo
author: Isidorus Hispalensis
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1403.tmp1403.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Sicque ex his consuetudo obtinuit pleraque ab auctoribus [AI. auctoritatibus] indifferenter accipi, quæ quidem quamvis similia videantur, quadam tamen propria inter se origine distinguuntur. De his apud Latinos Cato primus scripsit, ad cujus exemplum, ipse paucissimas partim edidi, partim ex auctorum libris deprompsi, tibique, lector, pro delectatione [legentium] subnotavi.
passages.english: And so from these [poets] the custom has prevailed that many words are taken by authors without distinction, words which, though they may seem similar, are nevertheless distinguished from one another by a certain origin of their own. Among the Latins Cato was the first to write about these; following his example, I myself have partly composed a very few, partly drawn [them] from the books of authors, and I have noted them down for you, reader, for the pleasure [of those who read].
passages.notes: Variant 'auctoritatibus' (authorities) for 'auctoribus' noted in the edition. The bracketed 'legentium' is an editorial addition.

passages.original: 17. Inter Amare et Digere putat differre Cicero, sæpiusque sic utitur, ut distinguat, atque amare ponat pro ardenter amare, at diligere pro levius amare, sicut in epistol, ad Brutum : Vate I in- quit, et nos ama ; vel , si id majus [Al., minus] est, dilige [ Al., diliges].
passages.english: 17. Between Amare and Diligere. Cicero thinks there is a difference, and often uses [them] so as to distinguish them, putting amare for loving ardently, but diligere for loving more lightly, as in the letter to Brutus: "Farewell," he says, "and love (ama) us too; or, if that is too much, be fond of (dilige) [us]."
passages.notes: 'Digere' in the heading is a scanning error for 'Diligere'; 'Vate' read as 'Vale' (farewell). Variant 'minus' for 'majus' and 'diliges' for 'dilige' noted in the edition. The Latin verbs are kept because the entry concerns the words themselves.

passages.original: 38. Inter Alvum et ventrem, et uterum. Alvus interius receptaculum cibi est, quo sordes defluunt, ut Sallustius, Simulans sibi alvum purgari. Venter est aspectus ipsius partis extrinsecus, ut Juvenalis : Montani quoque venter adest. Uterus autem proprie prægnantis est. Sed et hoc a poetis metri necessitate variatur.
passages.english: 38. Between alvus, venter and uterus. Alvus is the inner receptacle of food, through which waste flows out, as Sallust [says]: "Pretending that his bowels (alvus) were being purged." Venter is the outward appearance of that part, as Juvenal [says]: "Montanus's belly (venter) too is present." Uterus, however, properly belongs to a pregnant woman. But this too is varied by the poets through the necessity of metre.

passages.original: Aves dicimus quae per aera levibus [Al., levius] volitant pinnis [Al., pennis] , volucres autem non solum aves vocamus, sed quadrupedes nimia pernicitate currentes, sed tamen cum adjectione, ut puta volucrem equum, volucrem tigridem. Ut est illud Pacuvii : Volucri currit axe quadriga. Nam [Al., sed] et sagittae volucres dicuntur, quod his pinnæ [Al., pennae] conglutinantur. Nam sine adjectione tantum alitem sonat.
passages.english: We call "birds" (*aves*) those that flit through the air on light wings; but "winged" (*volucres*) we call not only birds but also four-footed animals that run with great swiftness, though only with a qualifying word added, as for example "a winged horse", "a winged tiger". As in that line of Pacuvius: "The four-horse chariot runs on winged axle." Indeed arrows too are called "winged", because feathers are glued to them. For without a qualifying word it denotes only a bird.
passages.notes: Bracketed alternative readings (Al.) in the edition are not translated; they do not materially change the sense.

passages.original: 9 48. Inter Anguem, serpentem et draconem. In mari angues, in terra serpenles, in templo dracones. Ut Virgilius : Tranquilla per alta angues ; et paulo post: Serpens amplexus uterque. Item : Delubra ad summa dracones.
passages.english: 48. Between anguis, serpens and draco. In the sea [they are] angues, on land serpentes, in a temple dracones. As Virgil [says]: "Snakes (angues) through the calm deep"; and a little later: "The serpent, embracing each"; and again: "The dragons (dracones) to the highest shrines."
passages.notes: The leading '9' is likely a page or footnote mark and is omitted; 'serpenles' read as 'serpentes'.

passages.original: 76. Inter Barbam et barbas. Barbam hominum, barlas pecudum vel herbarum dicimus. Barbas el hominum, ut apud Virgilium: Barbas incHOaque menta regis Romani.
passages.english: 76. Between barba and barbae. We say barba (singular) of men, barbae (plural) of cattle or plants. [But] barbae also of men, as in Virgil: "The beard (barbas) and grey chin of the Roman king."
passages.notes: 'barlas' read as 'barbas', 'el' as 'et'. 'incHOaque' is evidently 'incanaque' (and grey), as in Virgil's line.

passages.original: 79. loter Batsamum et opobalsamum. Balsamum est arbor ipsa, opobalsanlum succus collectus ex arbore. Nam opos dicitur succus. Probatio autem balsami, ut dicit Plinius, haec est: quod si contra solem feratur, et corruptum non sit, manum fereniis exurit.
passages.english: 79. Between balsamum and opobalsamum. Balsamum is the tree itself; opobalsamum is the juice collected from the tree, for opos means juice. The test of balsam, as Pliny says, is this: that if it is carried against the sun and is not adulterated, it burns the hand of the one carrying it.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'loter Batsamum' = 'Inter Balsamum', 'opobalsanlum' = 'opobalsamum', 'fereniis' = 'ferentis'.

passages.original: Inter Criminatorem et criminantem hoc interesse auctor Orbilius putat, quod criminator sit qui alteri crimen inferat, et id saepius faciat, criminans autem qui crimen inferat, et cum suspicione quoque id faciat quare quis magis noxius videatur. Ut Afranius : Non sum, inquit, tam criminosa [AI., criminosus], quam tu [AI., quantum], vipera, gannire ad aurem nunquam didici dominicam [Al., domini ].
passages.english: The authority Orbilius thinks the difference between a *criminator* and a *criminans* is this: a *criminator* is one who brings an accusation against another and does so repeatedly, while a *criminans* is one who brings an accusation and also does so with an insinuation by which someone may appear more guilty. As Afranius [says]: "I am not," she says, "as given to accusing as you, viper; I have never learned to yap into my master's ear."
passages.notes: Bracketed variants (criminosus, quantum, domini) would make the speaker masculine and alter the comparison slightly.

passages.original: Callidus est in disputando subdolus , versutus autem cujus mens in negotiorum actu ad quamlibet fraudem facile vertitur. Ergo callidum non pro astuto laUtum, 14 sed pro astute docto dicimus , versutum autem ab eo quod animum cito vertat. Unde et Plautus : Versutior es quam rota figularis [AI. figulari].
passages.english: [87. Between callidus and versutus.] Callidus is someone crafty in arguing; versutus is one whose mind, in the conduct of affairs, is easily turned to any fraud whatever. So we use callidus not for cunning in a bad sense, but for one cunningly learned; versutus, however, from the fact that he turns (vertat) his mind quickly. Hence Plautus too: "You are more versatile (versutior) than a potter's wheel."
passages.notes: 'laUtum' is corrupt; perhaps 'lautum' or a misreading (e.g. 'malum'); rendered by sense as 'cunning in a bad sense'. The '14' is a stray page mark and is omitted.

passages.original: 118. Inter Collum et cervicem. Collum [AI., Collus] semper cervicem, cervix jAI. collus] autem dum singulari numero dicitur, significat collum; dum plurali, superbiam, ut Cicero in Verrem (Lib. v): Prætorem tu acfusas ? Frange cervices.
passages.english: 118. Between collum and cervix. Collum always [means] the neck, but cervix, when it is used in the singular number, means the neck; when in the plural, pride, as Cicero [says] against Verres (Book 5): "Do you accuse a praetor? Break his neck (cervices)."
passages.notes: 'acfusas' read as 'accusas'. Variants 'collus' noted in the edition; in 'jAI. collus]' the 'j' is a misread bracket.

passages.original: Inter Domum et hospitium. Domus ad proprios habitatores pertinet. Nam hospitium tunc vocatur, cum aut aliquem recipimus aut cum ab aliqno ipsi recipimur; unde et qui venit, et ad quem venitur, hospes dicitur. Sic Plautus: Hospes necavit hospitem captum manu.
passages.english: [160.] Between domus and hospitium. A domus (home) belongs to its own inhabitants. For it is called hospitium (lodging) when either we receive someone or we ourselves are received by someone; hence both the one who comes and the one to whom he comes is called hospes (guest/host). So Plautus: "Host killed guest, taken by hand."
passages.notes: The Plautus line is obscure; 'captum manu' may mean 'caught by his own hand' or 'seized by force'.

passages.original: 179. Inter Eloquentem et loquacem. Sinceritas facundiae eloquentum est, effusa et incondita temeritas, loquacium. Unde cst Sallustius : Loquax magis quam facundus. Et Cicero: Hunc loquacem esse habitum, nunquam dissertum.
passages.english: 179. Between eloquens and loquax. Genuineness of speech belongs to the eloquent; a rashness that pours out and is disordered belongs to the talkative. Hence Sallust: "Talkative rather than eloquent." And Cicero: "This man was held to be talkative, never fluent (disertus)."
passages.notes: 'dissertum' read as 'disertum'.

passages.original: laudandum [F., laudaudo] extollunt, per unum f. Cicero : Nimium fortasse hæc illi eferunt.
passages.english: "[They] extol [someone] who is to be praised" [is written] with one f. Cicero: "Perhaps they extol these things too much."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-entry; the distinction (apparently between efferre and another verb spelled with ff) is lost. "[F., laudaudo]" is an editorial variant (laudaudo, apparently a misprint for laudando). "eferunt" is printed with a single f, as the entry requires.

passages.original: 26 194. Inter Exstinctum et restinctum. Exstinctum dicimus lumen, ut Cicero : Lumina civitatis exstincta sunt, restinctum vero incendium , ut idem Cicero : Subjectos prope jam ignes, circumdatosque restinxi- mus.
passages.english: 194. Between "extinguished" (exstinctum) and "put out" (restinctum). We say a light is "extinguished", as Cicero [says]: "The lights of the state have been extinguished"; but a fire is "put out", as the same Cicero [says]: "We have put out the fires that had almost been set beneath and around [us]."
passages.notes: The leading "26" is a line number from the printed page and has been omitted.

passages.original: 220. Inter Falsitatem et mendacium. Negare quod verum [Al., vere] est, falsitas est, fingere quod verum [Al., vere] non est, mendacium est. Unde 30 et Cato : Tu, inquam, si verum supprimis [Al., vera nobis supprimis], falsarius agnosceris; si falsa confingis, mendax esse videris [Al., judicaberis].
passages.english: 220. Between falsehood (falsitas) and lying (mendacium). To deny what is true is falsehood; to invent what is not true is lying. Hence Cato too [says]: "If, I say, you suppress the truth, you are recognised as a falsifier; if you invent falsehoods, you are seen to be a liar."
passages.notes: Variants noted by the edition: "vere" for "verum"; "vera nobis supprimis" ("you suppress true things from us"); "judicaberis" ("you will be judged") for "esse videris". The "30" is a line number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Fłuvius, perennis aquarum decursus generaliter, a flueudo dictus. Et proprie flumen ipsa aqua ; fluvius, eujus aqua ; torrens autem inde dictus, quia pluvia crescii, siccitate torrescit, id est, aresciL. Unde et Pacuvius : Flammeo vapore torrens torret. Porro rivus vocatur 33 qui subito ex pluvia fit, celeriterque decurrit ac deficit, fons autem est caput [Al., corpus] aquae nascentis. Amnis autem fluvius est nemore et [ Al., ex ] frondibus redimitus, et ex ipsa amoeniiale amnis vocatur.
passages.english: A river (*fluvius*) is, in general, a perennial running course of waters, named from flowing (*fluendo*). Properly, *flumen* is the water itself; *fluvius* [the thing] whose water [it is]; and a torrent (*torrens*) is so called because it swells with rain and is parched (*torrescit*) in drought, that is, dries up. Hence Pacuvius too: "Scorching (torrens) with fiery heat, it parches." Further, a *rivus* is the name for one that arises suddenly from rain, runs down quickly, and fails; a spring (*fons*) is the head of water as it rises. An *amnis*, however, is a river garlanded with woodland and foliage, and is called *amnis* from its very pleasantness (*amoenitas*).
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected (fluendo, cujus, crescit, arescit, praedicat, amoenitate). The stray "33" is a page number, omitted. The Pacuvius line could also be read "burning with fiery heat, it parches".

passages.original: 299. Inter Iniquitatem et peccatum sic distare dicit Ambrosius, quod iniquitas ad mentis acerbitatem refertur, peccatum vero ad prolapsionem corporis. Praecedit igitur iniquitas, peccatum sequitur. Sed gravior est iniquitas, tanquam materia peccatorum, in cujus comparatione levius est peccatum.
passages.english: 299. Ambrose says that iniquity and sin differ in this way: iniquity relates to bitterness of mind, while sin relates to a lapse of the body. So iniquity comes first and sin follows. But iniquity is the graver, being as it were the material of sins; compared with it, sin is lighter.

passages.original: 338. Inter Leges et jura. Jus dicitur, lex scribitur. Unde et Virgilius : Jura dabat legesque viris. Item leges humanae, jura 45 divina sunt. Ideoque et juramentum dicitur id est, sacramentum in Deo [Al., Domino]. Hinc et Virgilius ; Fas mihi Graiorum sacrata resolvere jura.
passages.english: 338. Between laws (leges) and rights (jura). A right is spoken, a law is written. Hence Virgil too [says]: "He was giving rights and laws to the men." Again, laws are human, rights are divine. And for that reason an oath (juramentum) is so called, that is, a sacred bond in God. Hence Virgil too [says]: "It is lawful for me to dissolve the sacred oaths of the Greeks."
passages.notes: The edition gives the variant "Domino" ("in the Lord") for "Deo". The "45" is a line number and has been omitted. In the second Virgil quotation, "jura" is better taken as "bonds" or "oaths".

passages.original: Inter Locum religiosum, et sacrum, et sandum, quod sacrum vocamus, quod ad deos superos pertinet; religiosum , quod ad deos inferos ; sanctum vero, quod aliqua sanctitate sanctum est, ut eunt tauri apud Homerum ('οδυσσ. μ) soli sancti, sacri, sacrosancti.
passages.english: Between a religious place (religiosus), a sacred one (sacer), and a holy one (sanctus). We call "sacred" what belongs to the gods above; "religious" what belongs to the gods below; and "holy" what is holy by some sanctity, as the bulls in Homer (Odyssey 12) are alone holy, sacred, sacrosanct.
passages.notes: "sandum" has been read as "sanctum". "eunt" is probably a corruption of "sunt" or "erant". The sentence is awkwardly constructed, possibly corrupt.

passages.original: 388. Inter Nomen, prænomen, cognomen et agnomen. Nomen [Al., prænomen] est vocabulum propriæ appellationis ; prænomen, quod numinibus. ob dignitatem [Al., dignitate] generis præponitur; ut Publius Virgilius., Non enim; possumus dicere [Al., .dicimus] Virgilius Publius. Cognomen, quode ex familia generis venit, ut puta Scipio Cornelius, a Corne- lia familia ortus.. Agnomen, 51 quod ex virtute, vel vitio trahitur.: ut Scipio Africanus, pro eo quod Africam vicerit: vel Lentulus Sura,'pro co quod majores habuerat.
passages.english: 388. Between name, praenomen, cognomen and agnomen. The name is the word of one's proper designation; the praenomen is what is placed before names on account of the dignity of the family, as Publius Virgilius. For we cannot say Virgilius Publius. The cognomen is what comes from the family of the lineage, as for example Scipio Cornelius, sprung from the Cornelian family. The agnomen is what is drawn from a virtue or a vice, as Scipio Africanus, because he conquered Africa; or Lentulus Sura, because he had large
passages.notes: Bracketed [Al., ...] are editorial variant readings, not translated. 'numinibus' read as 'nominibus'. The sentence ends mid-phrase: 'majores ... suras' (large calves) continues in following context.

passages.original: Nefarius, ut Yarro existimat , non dignus farre. Quo primo cibi genere vita hominum sustentabatur [Al., sustinebatur]. Nefandus, id est, nec nominandus quidem. Profanus autem , cui sacris non licet interesse. De quo Sallustius : Sacra polluet profanus. Profanns ergo, porro, id est, longe a fano.
passages.english: Nefarius ("wicked"), as Varro thinks, [means] not worthy of spelt (far), the first kind of food by which human life was sustained. Nefandus ("unspeakable"), that is, not even to be named. Profanus ("profane"), however, [is] one who is not permitted to take part in sacred rites. Of him Sallust [says]: "The profane man will pollute the rites." So profanus [is like] porro ("far off"), that is, far from the shrine (fanum).
passages.notes: "Yarro" has been read as "Varro" and "Profanns" as "Profanus". The edition gives the variant "sustinebatur" for "sustentabatur".

passages.original: 431. Inter Passionem et propassionem Hieronymus in Matthæum distinguit, dicens : quod passio repu. tatur in culpa ; propassio, licet culpam habeat [AI., pro culpa habeatur], tamen non tenetur [Al., retine- tur] in crimine. Ergo qui viderit mulierem, et anima ejus fuerit titillata, hic propassione percussus est : Si vero consenserit, et de cogitatione affectum fecerit (sicut scriptum est in David : transierunt in affectum cordis), de propassionc transit ad passionem, et huic non voluntas deest, sed occasio.
passages.english: 431. Jerome, on Matthew, distinguishes between passion (passio) and pre-passion (propassio), saying that passion is counted as a fault, while pre-passion, although it involves fault, is nevertheless not held as a crime. So whoever sees a woman and whose soul is stirred has been struck by pre-passion; but if he consents and turns the thought into desire (as is written in David: "they passed into the desire of the heart"), he passes from pre-passion to passion, and in his case it is not the will that is lacking, but the opportunity.
passages.notes: Variants noted by the edition: "pro culpa habeatur" ("is regarded as a fault") and "retinetur" for "tenetur".

passages.original: 432. Inter Percunctationem et interrogationem Augustinus hoc interesse 56 existimat, dicens : quod ad percunctationem multa responderi soleant, veluti quid est hoc, aut illud? ut respondeantur diversa, vel varia. Ad interrogationem non multa respondentur, sed aut non, aut etiam pronuntiabitur.
passages.english: 432. Augustine thinks the difference between inquiry (percunctatio) and question (interrogatio) is this, saying: to an inquiry many answers are usually given, for example "What is this, or that?", so that different or various things are answered. To a question not many answers are given, but either "no" or "yes" will be said.
passages.notes: The "56" is a line number and has been omitted.

passages.original: 440. Inter Properare et festinare. Marcus Cato sic distinguit dicens : Qui unumquodque mature transigit, is properat. Qui multa simul incipit, neque perficit , is festinat. Ego unumquodque quod adortus eram transigebam o.
passages.english: 440. Between properare and festinare (both "to hurry"). Marcus Cato distinguishes them thus, saying: "He who completes each thing in good time 'makes haste' (properat). He who begins many things at once and does not finish them 'rushes' (festinat). I completed each thing that I had undertaken."
passages.notes: The final "o" appears to be a stray footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: Sic portentum dicitur a portendendo, id est porro ostendendo, sicut et prodigium, quod porro dicat, id est fulura de longe praedical. Monstrum sane a monitu vel monstrando dictum, quod aliquid significando demonstret et .statim. Quinque sunt autem genera prodigiorum, ut Varro dicit, id est: portentum, ostentum, prodigium, miraculum et monstrum.
passages.english: So a portent (*portentum*) is named from portending, that is, showing forward, as also a prodigy (*prodigium*), because it speaks forward, that is, foretells things to come from afar. A monster (*monstrum*), certainly, is named from warning (*monitu*) or showing (*monstrando*), because by signifying something it points it out at once. There are, as Varro says, five kinds of prodigies, that is: *portentum*, *ostentum*, *prodigium*, *miraculum* and *monstrum*.
passages.notes: "fulura" and "praedical" read as futura, praedicat.

passages.original: 485. Inter Recens et novum. Recens nascitur; novum fit. Unde et Virgilius : Lac mihi non aestate novum, non frigore defit.
passages.english: 485. Between "recent" (recens) and "new" (novum). What is recent is born; what is new is made. Hence Virgil too: "I lack no new milk, neither in summer nor in cold."

passages.original: 500. Inter Stultum, fatuum, et stupidum. Quidam veterum fatuum existimant qui nec quod fatur ipse, nec quod alii dicunt, intelligat; stultum vero hebetiorem corde. Unde Afranius : Ego, inquit, me stultum existimo, fatuum esse non opinor. Id est, obtusis quidem sensibus, non tamen nullis. Stupidus vero dictus est quasi lapideus, quasi stolidus.
passages.english: 500. Between *stultus* (foolish), *fatuus* (silly), and *stupidus* (stupid). Some of the ancients consider *fatuus* one who understands neither what he himself says (*fatur*) nor what others say; but *stultus* one rather dull of mind. Hence Afranius: "I consider myself," he says, "foolish; I do not think I am silly." That is, with blunted senses, yet not with none. *Stupidus*, however, is so called as if stony, as if *stolidus* (dull).

passages.original: 507. Inter Sceleratum, scelestum, et scelerosum. Grammatici dicunt sceleratum illum esse in quo fit [Al., sit] scelus ; ut Cicero : 0 te [AI., tu] scelerate, qui subactus et prostitutus ea, Scelestum autem per quem fit. Ut Terentius : scelesta, ovem lupo commisisti. Scelerosus, qui facit: ut idem : Ego illum scelerosum misera nolens pertuli. Sed haec auctores non usquequaque custodiunt.
passages.english: 507. Between sceleratus, scelestus and scelerosus. The grammarians say that sceleratus is the one against whom a crime is done [variant: in whom crime is], as Cicero: "O you wicked one, who, subdued and prostituted, [...] these things." Scelestus, however, is the one through whom it is done, as Terence: "Wicked woman, you have entrusted the sheep to the wolf." Scelerosus is the one who does it, as the same [author]: "Wretched me, against my will I have put up with that criminal." But authors do not observe these [distinctions] everywhere.
passages.notes: The Cicero quotation is cut off in the text ("ea" leaves the clause incomplete). Variant readings noted by the edition: "sit" for "fit", "tu" for "te".

passages.original: IV) : Hunc ego si potui tantum sperare dolorem ; dum omne quod exhorret animus rectius timere dicatur [Al. add. quam sperare]. Sed grammatici hoc exponunt, dicentes : Sperare dixit pro timere. Quod et Lucanus distinguens ait : Liceat sperare timenti.
passages.english: IV): "If I have been able to hope for (sperare) so great a grief"; whereas everything that the mind shudders at would more correctly be said to be feared [variant adds: than hoped for]. But the grammarians explain this, saying: he said "hope" in place of "fear". Lucan, too, making the distinction, says: "Let the one who fears be allowed to hope."
passages.notes: Passage begins mid-sentence; the reference is to Aeneid book IV, as the preceding context shows.

passages.original: 515. Inter Simulare et dissimulare. Dissimulamus nota : simulamus ignota. Qui enim fingit se scire quod nescit, simulat; 66 qui autem quod scit nescire se dicit, dissimulat. Unde et Sallustius : llle simulator incerti, ac certi dissimulator erat.
passages.english: 515. Between simulare and dissimulare. We dissimulate things known; we simulate things unknown. For one who pretends to know what he does not know simulates; but one who says he does not know what he knows dissimulates. Hence Sallust too: "He was a pretender to what was uncertain and a concealer of what was certain."
passages.notes: "66" is a page number from the printed edition, omitted.

passages.original: 516. Inter Sistere, et consistere, et assistere. Sistere est interdum resistere, vel prohibere, id est, qui aliquam rem in loco stare facit. Ut Virgilius : Sistere aquam fluviis. Assistere vero et ante unum, et coram multis ; consistere in medio adesse.
passages.english: 516. Between sistere, consistere and assistere. Sistere is sometimes to resist or to prevent, that is, [said of] one who makes something stand in a place, as Virgil: "to stop the water in the rivers." Assistere, however, [is used both] before one person and in the presence of many; consistere [means] to be present in the middle.

passages.original: Solium autem, vel a solius sessione, vel a soliditate dictum. Solium Latini, Græci tharonum dicunt. Sedes autem dictæ, quia apud veteres Romanos non erat usus accumbendi. Unde et consedere antiquo more dicitur. Nam veteres sedentes epulabantur. Postea, ut ait Varro, de Yila populi Romani, viri discumbere coeperunt, mulieres sedere. Quia turpe illis erat discumbere mulierem [AI., discumbere visumj.
passages.english: The *solium* (throne), however, is named either from the sitting of one alone (*solius*) or from solidity. What Latins call *solium*, Greeks call *thronos*. Seats (*sedes*), moreover, are so named because among the ancient Romans there was no custom of reclining. Hence too "to sit together" is said after the ancient manner. For the ancients ate their meals sitting. Later, as Varro says in *On the Life of the Roman People*, men began to recline, women to sit, because it seemed shameful to them for a woman to recline.
passages.notes: "tharonum" read as thronum; "Yila" as Vita. A variant reads "because reclining seemed shameful to them".

passages.original: Senectus est gravior ætas post juventutem succedens, senium autem ultima ætas post gravitatem veniens. Sic senex et senior. Nam senior adhuc viridior. Ut illud Virgilianum : Jam senior, sed cruda deo viridisque senectus. Et Terentius : Quo jure sum usus adolescentior; non utique magis adolescens, sed minus. Ut senior, minus senex. Senecta autem est ipsa sors, sive [ Al., atque] conditio senectuti accedens.
passages.english: Senectus (old age) is the heavier age that follows after youth, while senium is the final age that comes after that heaviness. So too senex and senior: for a senior is still rather vigorous, as in that Virgilian line: "Now older, but the god's old age is fresh and green." And Terence: "The right I enjoyed when younger (adolescentior)"; that is, not more a youth, but less. So senior [means] less an old man. Senecta, however, is the very lot or [variant: and] condition that attaches to old age.

passages.original: 71 561. Inter Testor , contestor, et obtestor. Testor saepenumero ad jusjurandum pertinet, ut Virgilius, per sidera testor; contestor autem ad judices, obtestor ad adversarios.
passages.english: 561. Between testor, contestor and obtestor. Testor very often pertains to an oath, as Virgil: "I swear by the stars"; contestor, however, [pertains] to judges, obtestor to adversaries.
passages.notes: "71" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: Facies est natu- ralis oris habitus immutabilis, vultus vero pro rerum ac temporum qualitate varius et mutabilis [Al., commutabilis], et secundum affectionem animi modo lætus, modo tristis. Unde et vultuosi dicuntur qui vultum saepe commotaM. Itaque Lucilius haec quasi distinguens ait: Quæ focies, qui vultus viro. Dicimus autem et vultum coeli et vultum maris, quia et mare saepe in varios motus ventorum flatibus mutatur, et celi vultus ex luce in tenebras, et ex sereno in nubilum commutatur, sicut et hominum cum mentibus vultus.
passages.english: The face (*facies*) is the natural, unchangeable bearing of the countenance; but the expression (*vultus*) is various and changeable according to the nature of circumstances and times, and in accordance with the feeling of the mind is now glad, now sad. Hence too people are called *vultuosi* who often change their expression. And so Lucilius, as if distinguishing these, says: "What a face, what an expression the man has!" We speak also of the countenance of the sky and the countenance of the sea, because the sea too is often changed into various motions by the blasts of the winds, and the sky's countenance changes from light to darkness and from clear to cloudy, just as men's expressions change with their minds.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (commutant, facies, caeli). The Lucilius fragment is brief and its exact construal uncertain.

passages.original: 51. hi capite autem, ut ait sanctus Augustinus, Tres tanquam ventriculi cerebri constituti sunt : unus anterior ad faciem, a quo sensus omnis; alter posterior ad servicem, a quo motus omnis ; tertius inter utrumque, in quo memoria vigere demonstratur, ne cum sensum sequitur molus, non connectat homo quod faciendum est, si fuerit oblitus quod fecit.
passages.english: 51. In the head, however, as Saint Augustine says, three ventricles of the brain, as it were, have been set: one at the front, toward the face, from which comes all sensation; another at the back, toward the neck, from which comes all movement; a third between the two, in which memory is shown to thrive, lest, when movement follows sensation, a person fail to connect what must be done, if he has forgotten what he has done.
passages.notes: Read "In capite" for "hi capite", "cervicem" for "servicem", "motus" for "molus".

passages.original: 82. Jam vero mediae aetatis proprie dicuntur vir et mulier. 94 Vir itaque nuncupatus, ut ait Lactantius, quia major in eo vis sit quam in feminis, et hinc virtus nomen accipit. Item mulier a mollitie dicta, immutata et detracta littera, quasi mollier.
passages.english: 82. Now those of middle age are properly called vir (man) and mulier (woman). Vir, then, was so named, as Lactantius says, because there is greater strength (vis) in him than in women, and from this virtus (virtue) takes its name. Likewise mulier is so called from softness (mollities), with a letter changed and removed, as if mollier.
passages.notes: "94" is a page number, omitted.

passages.original: 84. Extremae jam aetatis, senes et anus vocantur. Senes autem quidam dictos putant, eo quod se nesciunt, et per nimiam ætatem delirent atque dcsipiant. Unde et Plato : In pueris erescit ser- sus, in juvenibus viget, in senibus minuitur. Anus autem ex multis annis dicta est, quasi annosa.
passages.english: 84. Those of the final age are called senes (old men) and anus (old women). Some think senes are so called because they do not know themselves (se nesciunt), and through excessive age become delirious and foolish. Hence Plato too: "In boys sense grows, in young men it flourishes, in old men it diminishes." Anus, however, is so called from many years (anni), as if annosa.
passages.notes: Read "desipiant" and "crescit sensus" for scanning errors.

passages.original: 94. Inter animum et animam Lactantius distinguere philosophos quosdam ita existimat: < Quidam, inquit, aiunt aliud esse animam qua vivimus; aliud animum quo sentimus et sapimus, quia, valente in corpore anilua, nonnunquam animus perit, sicut accidere dementibus solet.
passages.english: 94. Lactantius considers that certain philosophers distinguish between *animus* [mind] and *anima* [soul] in this way: "Some," he says, "say that the soul by which we live is one thing, and the mind by which we perceive and are wise is another, because, while the soul remains strong in the body, the mind sometimes perishes, as usually happens to the insane.
passages.notes: "anilua" is a scanning error for "anima". The quotation opened with "<" is not closed within the passage.

passages.original: 166. Sequitur tristitia , cujus tria sunt genera, quarum prima, ut ait Cassianus , temperata et rationabilis, de delictorum pœnitudine veniens; altera perturbata, irralionabilis, de anxietate mentis seu desperatione peccatorum exoriens; tertia de iracundia, vel de illato damno, vel desiderio praepedito procedens.
passages.english: 166. Next follows sadness, of which there are three kinds. The first of these, as Cassian says, is measured and reasonable, arising from repentance for offences; the second is disordered and unreasonable, springing from anxiety of mind or despair over sins; the third proceeds from anger, or from a loss inflicted, or from a thwarted desire.
passages.notes: "irralionabilis" is read as "irrationabilis".
